newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire fighting no direct threat to Shaba mines.
newsitem.headline: Zaire fighting no direct threat to Shaba mines.

text.p: Fighting linked to a Tutsi-led revolt in the east poses no direct threat to Zaire's copper and cobalt mines in Shaba but spreading chaos or delays in promised elections may rekindle separatist desires.
The southern region has been spared both the fighting and the political disturbances which erupted across much of the huge Central African state after the revolt began on October 18.
"Security has been tightened, particularly with possible mining deals in the offing, but we have found no threat," said one regional government official.
"When students planned to demonstrate against the government we just told them it would not look good and they stopped."
Rebels led by Shaba-born Laurent Kabila have driven the army back from a strip along the Rwandan and Burundian border, capturing the major towns of Goma and Bukavu.

But although the rebels are close to Shaba's northern boundary they are still at least 1,000 km (600 miles) from the mining centres, and given the state of Zaire's roads that means at least a week, maybe a month, by truck.
Known by those of its people who want more autonomy as Katanga, the region does not have a recent history of stability.

Isolated from the capital by a distance of 1500 km (950 miles), resentment is barely hidden at the drain on mining recepits which leaves little for local people but a few poorly paid jobs at state-run Gecamines.

"Everyone knows they would be much better off if Katanga were autonomous, but we have not opted for violence, we have opted for elections," said Lukonde Kyenge, regional leader of the Union of Federalists and Independent Republicans (UFERI).
"There is a threat from the fighting, but not directly. The same causes have the same effects, and if you do not look after the provinces then this is what you get."

UFERI and its outspoken leader, Kyungu wa Kumwanza, have a large degree of popular support in Shaba, although it is not so visible since Kyungu was suspended as governor in 1995 after accusations that he was importing arms for a new secession bid.

An attempt to break away from Zaire just after the dawn of independence from Belgium in 1960 was put down by the central government after years of long and bloody war in which Mobutu Sese Seko, president since 1965, played a central role.
Fighting erupted again in the 1970s and was only put down with the help of French, Belgian and Moroccan troops.

In 1992 ethnic violence targeting migrants from neighbouring Kasai region caused many to flee and was almost the death knell for Gecamines in 1993 as 10,000 workers fled and copper and cobalt production slumped.
The fact that the leader of the new rebel movement has his origins in Shaba has raised fears that instability might once again spread to his home region.
Lukonde said that the regional ties had already caused some of the authorities to point fingers at UFERI.
"We are not directly concerned. Kabila left here over 30 years ago and we don't know him," said Lukonde.
"Elections will give us the federalism we want and if they are not held across the country next year we will hold them by ourselves and go our own way."
Mobutu bowed to foreign and internal pressure for reform in 1990 but Zaire's democratic transition has dragged. The oft-postponed deadline for elections is now July 1997.

Shaba already has a substantial degree of autonomy as a result of the steady collapse of national infrastructures through years of corruption and mismanagement and in trade terms looks much more to Zambia and South Africa than to Kinshasa.

Foreign mining companies are showing serious interest in exploiting Shaba's huge resources for the first time in decades, after the near collapse of Gecamines forced it to look for outside help and coincided with a general liberalising trend.

Copper production at an estimated 42,000 tonnes in 1996 is less than a tenth of what it was at its peak in the mid-1980s, but with investment in new technology analysts say Shaba could produce even more than it did then.

"I don't know about the countryside but at least in Lubumbashi people can see that if investment comes in then there are likely to be more jobs, more money. They don't want to threaten that," said schoolteacher Benoit Nsenga.
